lines.text: You wake up and your knees hurt.
Not a little.
Like someone replaced them overnight with rusty hinges.
You sit up and your back makes a sound
like a bag of popcorn.
You reach for your glasses.
You don't wear glasses, but they're on the nightstand,
and when you put them on,
the world finally comes into focus.
You walk to the bathroom mirror
and an 83-year-old man looks back at you.
White hair, deep lines around the eyes,
hands covered in brown spots,
and in his eyes,
exactly the same scared look you had yesterday
when you were 16.
Your mom knocks on the door.
Honey, you're going to be late for school.
You open it.
She looks at you for three seconds,
and she says very calmly,
okay, we'll figure this out,
because here's the part you don't know yet.
Tomorrow morning, you're going to wake up
at a different age,
and the day after that, another one.
Every morning for the next 100 days,
a number will be picked,
and you won't know what it is
until you look in the mirror.
By the end, you'll understand the rule behind it,
and the last morning will be an age nobody expects.
But first, you need a cane and a ride to school.
Day one, your best friend Eli sees you at the bus stop
and drops his skateboard.
Dude, is that you?
You nod.
He walks around you twice, slowly.
That's the coolest thing I've ever seen.
Then he asks if you can buy him an energy drink.
At 83, you can buy anything you want,
and nobody asks any questions.
You're a very convincing old man.
In the cafeteria, the lunch lady gives you
the senior discount before you even ask.
In class, your history teacher
asks what the world was like in 1950.
You make something up.
The whole class takes notes.
Here's what's strange.
You can still run through every math formula
you learned last week.
Your brain is exactly the same.
Only your body is different.
And that body has some surprises.
By the time people reach their 80s,
nearly half of them have some hearing loss.
At lunch, you can't hear Eli talk over the noise.
You nod and say, mm-hmm, to everything.
He tells you his dog died.
You say, mm-hmm, he's stunned.
You spend the whole afternoon trying to fix it.
By evening, your legs are shaking.
You go to bed at 7.30.
Day two, you open your eyes,
and the ceiling looks enormous.
You try to sit up and almost fall out of bed.
Your legs are too short.
You walk to the bathroom,
and the sink is above your head.
You climb on the toilet to look in the mirror.
A six-year-old stares back.
Round cheeks, missing front tooth,
hair sticking straight up.
You try to say, this is a disaster.
What comes out is, fifth is a disaster.
Your mom comes in,
and she doesn't look surprised anymore.
She just kneels down and says, hey, buddy, pancakes?
And here's the strangest part.
You still think like a 16-year-old,
but your body doesn't.
A six-year-old's brain is completely different.
By age five, a child's brain is already
about 90% of its adult size.
But the parts that handle self-control,
the parts that say, don't scream, you're in public.
Those parts are barely finished.
They won't finish until your mid-20s.
So when mom puts your pancakes down
and the syrup runs off the plate and onto the floor,
you burst into tears.
Real, loud, ugly tears.
You know it's stupid.
You know it's syrup.
Your brain says, calm down.
Your body says, the syrup is gone and the world is over.
Mom hugs you anyway.
She doesn't say it's okay.
She just says, I know.
At school, you can't write your name.
A tiny boy named Danny shares his Pokemon cards with you,
and you spend 20 minutes watching a snail on the playground.
It's the best 20 minutes you've had all month.
Day three, 41.
You wake up in a body that feels completely normal,
strong, steady, a little tired.
Your back has a small ache.
You have a mortgage-sized worry in your chest
and you don't know where it came from.
You go downstairs.
Your mom is sitting at the kitchen table,
even though it's two in the morning.
Bill's spread out in front of her.
She jumps when she sees you.
Oh, you're, how old are you today?
She laughs, a tired laugh.
You sit down across from her
and something happens that has never happened before.
She doesn't treat you like her kid.
She treats you like a person.
She slides one of the bills across the table.
Honestly, I don't know how we're going to pay for this.
You've never heard her say that, not once.
In 16 years, she's always had an answer.
You sit with her until the sun comes up.
You go through every bill line by line.
She tells you about her day.
Her boss, how tired she is,
how much she misses her mom.
You listen for the first time you hear her.
At 6 a.m., she puts her head on your shoulder.
I'm glad it's you, she says.
Whatever this is, I'm glad it's you.
You don't know it yet,
but this is the first clue.
Over the next week, you learn how to use it
and you start to get greedy.
At 19, you finish a race in the top 10.
At 23, you fix your mom's credit card problem
in one phone call.
At 70, you go to the movies for half price.
At eight, you get into the zoo for free.
The human body is a strange machine.
Babies are born with about 300 bones.
By adulthood, many of them fuse
and you're down to 206.
At two years old, you can touch your toes to your ears.
At 60, you can't touch your toes at all.
So, you start planning.
You write the ages in a notebook.
Which age is best for exams?
Which age is best for sports?
Which age gets you into places you shouldn't be?
You're proud of yourself.
You feel like you've solved a puzzle.
Then, you fail a test.
You wake up at four years old
on the morning of a math exam.
You can't hold a pen.
You can't read the questions.
Your teacher looks at you with real sympathy,
hands you crayons and writes a zero.
Your grades fall off a cliff.
You miss four basketball practices in a row.
The coach tells you, we can't count on you.
Which is fair.
And then, there's Ruth.
Ruth sits two rows ahead of you in English.
For two years, you've wanted to talk to her.
On day 20, you wake up at 16,
your real age, and you finally get the courage.
She laughs at your joke.
She asks if you wanna get ice cream after school.
The next morning, you wake up at 45.
She walks up to you at your locker
and she looks at you.
A middle-aged man in a hoodie
standing in the hallway of a high school.
She smiles awkwardly.
She backs away.
She tells her friends,
she's not sure what's going on with you anymore.
By the end of the week, nobody sits with you at lunch.
Eli does, but only because he's your best friend
and even he looks tired.
I just never know who I'm talking to, he says.
I don't know if I'm supposed to talk to you
like a kid or a grown-up or a grandpa.
I don't know either, you say.
By day 50, you're angry.
You never get to be one person.
You start talking back to the mirror.
Why can't it just stop?
The mirror doesn't answer, but your neighbor does.
His name is Mr. Okafor.
He lives alone next door and he's 83.
You've never really talked to him.
Today, you wake up at 83 too.
You step out onto the porch,
ashamed and annoyed,
and he's on the next porch
in a chair that's too big for him, looking at the street.
Rough morning, he asks.
You say something rude.
You don't remember what.
He doesn't flinch.
I've had that face for a while, he says.
You get used to it.
And then he starts to talk
about his wife who died six years ago,
about his kids who live in other cities,
about the fact that nobody asks him anything anymore.
People talk to him the way you talk to a lamp.
They say, how are you?
But they don't wait for the answer.
Studies of older adults often find that day to day,
they report being at least as happy as the young.
But that doesn't mean they aren't lonely.
Many are.
And loneliness hurts the body too.
You stay on the porch until the sun goes down.
When you leave, he says, thank you.
Nobody's sat here in years.
The next morning, you wake up at six.
And that's when you notice the pattern.
Danny, the boy with the Pokemon cards, is six.
He's smaller than the other kids.
Yesterday, some older boys took his backpack.
And today, you're six in his class,
walking right next to him.
When the boys come back, you stand there,
small and shaking, and say, you can't.
And because you're a six-year-old, they laugh.
But they don't touch him
because two six-year-olds are harder to bully than one.
Then you remember the porch.
Mr. Okafor was 83.
You woke up at 83.
You remember your mom at the kitchen table
at two in the morning.
She was 41.
You woke up at 41.
You open your notebook.
For 53 mornings, you wrote down your age
and what happened that day.
You flip through the pages.
Now you see it.
Every single age matches someone who needed you that day.
The age wasn't random.
It was the age of the person
who most needed somebody exactly like that.
You weren't cursed.
You were being sent.
After that, you stop trying to plan.
You stop looking at the mirror with dread.
Every morning, you check your age, and then you go looking.
At 30, you help a woman at a bus stop
with a broken suitcase and no money.
At 15, you sit with a new kid in the cafeteria.
At 57, you help a man who just lost his job fill out forms.
At 94, you hold a stranger's hand in a hospital waiting room.
They never learn your name.
Eli notices first.
You're different, he says.
Even when you're old, even when you're six,
you're like more here.
For the first time in weeks, you smile.
Then comes day 100.
You wake up.
You don't look in the mirror right away.
You stand in your room.
Your knees don't hurt.
Your back doesn't ache.
Your hands look like your hands.
You walk to the bathroom slowly, and you look.
16, your real age.
The same messy hair, the same tired eyes.
You wait.
You get dressed.
You check your notebook.
You check the street.
You walk next door and knock on Mr. Okafor's door.
He's fine.
He's making toast.
You go to Danny's.
Danny is fine.
His mom thanks you for yesterday.
For the first time in 100 days, nobody needs you.
You sit on the back steps, confused.
And then slowly, you understand.
For 100 days, you were every age.
For everyone.
Sick, scared, old, young, lonely, strong.
And not once, not on a single morning,
were you just you.
Today, the age is 16.
The person who meets someone 16 is you.
You hear the door behind you.
Your mom sits next to you on the step in her work uniform.
She's holding two cups of hot chocolate.
She puts one in your hands.
I called in sick, she says.
You never call in sick.
I know.
She looks at the yard.
100 days of you taking care of everyone.
Nobody asked how you were doing.
You open your mouth to say, I'm fine.
You stop.
You've learned that much.
I'm tired, you say.
I'm really, really tired.
And your mom, who's 41,
and who has been holding the world together for 16 years,
pulls you close and says the only thing there is to say.
I know.
Tell me.
So you do.
All of it.
The mornings, the mirror, the fear.
You talk for four hours.
She doesn't say a word.
When you're done, the hot chocolate has gone cold
and the sun is high.
You never wake up as someone else again.
But sometimes when you see a person alone at a bus stop
or an old man on a porch
or a kid with no one to sit with,
you feel a little strange.
Like you're 16 and 83 and six all at once.
So if you had to wake up at a different age
every morning, would you want to?
What's the one age you'd love to be for a day?
Tell us in the comments.
And if you'd have spent that day with Mr. Okafor,
hit like and subscribe for more What Ifs.
